lessons.title: Radiation: Risks and Benefits
lessons.description: Ionising and non-ionising radiation, exposure risk, and how we use radiation to help people.
lessons.content_html:
Radiation All Around Us

Radiation is part of daily life. We are constantly exposed to background radiation from rocks (particularly granite), from cosmic rays from space, from radon gas in the air, from food and drink, and from medical procedures. This background dose varies by location — living in Cornwall exposes you to more radon than living in London, because granite rock releases more of this naturally occurring radioactive gas.

Not all radiation is the same. The key distinction for understanding risk is whether the radiation is ionising or non-ionising. Ionising radiation carries enough energy to knock electrons away from atoms, turning them into ions. This can damage or destroy cells and, if it alters DNA, may trigger cancer. Non-ionising radiation does not have enough energy to ionise atoms, though some forms (such as UV) can still cause harm at high doses.

Key Fact

Ionising radiation: alpha (\(\alpha\)), beta (\(\beta\)) and gamma (\(\gamma\)) from radioactive materials, plus X-rays. Non-ionising: UV, infrared, microwaves, radio waves. Ionising radiation is far more dangerous because it can damage DNA directly.

Types of Ionising Radiation

Alpha, beta and gamma differ in penetrating power and ionising ability — and these differences determine both their hazards and their uses:

• Alpha (\(\alpha\)): a helium nucleus (2 protons + 2 neutrons). Strongly ionising because its large charge and mass interact intensely with matter. Stopped by a few centimetres of air or a sheet of paper. Cannot penetrate skin, so an external alpha source poses little risk to internal organs — but if an alpha-emitting substance is inhaled or swallowed, the radiation delivers its full energy to sensitive tissue close by.
• Beta (\(\beta\)): a fast-moving electron. Moderately ionising. Penetrates paper but stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium. Can penetrate a short distance into body tissue.
• Gamma (\(\gamma\)): a high-energy electromagnetic wave. Weakly ionising but highly penetrating — passes through the body and is only significantly absorbed by dense lead or thick concrete. This penetrating power makes it useful for both medical imaging and radiotherapy, but means external gamma sources are hazardous from a distance.
• X-rays: also electromagnetic, similar to gamma but produced by electron transitions in machines rather than by nuclear decay. Similar penetrating power to gamma.

How Radiation Harms the Body

Ionising radiation harms cells in two main ways. At high doses, it kills cells directly — this is what causes radiation sickness and burns in severe accidents. At lower doses, it can alter DNA without killing the cell. A mutated cell may then divide uncontrollably, potentially causing cancer. The radiation dose received is the key factor: the higher the dose and the longer the exposure time, the greater the risk. This is why medical imaging doses are kept as low as possible while still providing a useful image.

It is important to distinguish between contamination and irradiation. Contamination means a radioactive substance is on or inside the body, continuing to deliver radiation that cannot be stopped simply by moving away. Irradiation means being exposed to radiation from an external source; once the source is removed the exposure stops and the person does not become radioactive. Contamination is generally considered more dangerous because the exposure is continuous and the substance may be inside the body where even alpha particles can reach sensitive tissue.

Key Fact

Contamination (radioactive material in/on the body) is more dangerous than irradiation (external exposure) because the source continues to deliver radiation internally, even from alpha particles that cannot penetrate skin from outside.

Beneficial Uses of Radiation

The same properties that make radiation hazardous also make it medically and industrially useful. Every use involves a risk–benefit judgement that depends on the specific situation.

X-rays in medical imaging: X-rays penetrate soft tissue but are absorbed by denser material like bone and metal. A dental X-ray exposes the patient to a fraction of the dose of a chest X-ray, and a chest X-ray delivers a dose roughly equivalent to a few days of background radiation. The benefit — diagnosing broken bones, tooth decay, or tumours — is very likely to outweigh the small additional risk for most patients. Pregnant women and children are treated more cautiously because their cells are dividing rapidly and are more vulnerable.

Radiotherapy: high doses of gamma rays or focused X-rays (or sometimes beta-emitting implants) target cancerous tumours. The beam is directed from several angles so that healthy surrounding tissue receives only a fraction of the dose that the tumour receives. The benefit — destroying a life-threatening cancer — must be weighed against the risk of damage to healthy tissue and the small risk of triggering a secondary cancer years later. For most cancer patients, the benefit substantially outweighs the risk.

Radioactive tracers: a gamma-emitting radioactive substance with a short half-life (such as technetium-99m, which has a half-life of around 6 hours) is introduced into the body. Because gamma rays penetrate the body, their path can be tracked externally, allowing doctors to image organ function. The short half-life means the patient’s dose is minimised — the isotope decays to negligible levels within a day.

Sterilisation: gamma rays kill bacteria on medical equipment and can be used to extend the shelf life of food. The food does not become radioactive — gamma radiation passes through it without leaving any radioactive material behind.

Smoke detectors are a familiar everyday use. They contain a tiny source of alpha radiation (americium-241). Alpha particles ionise air molecules, creating a small electrical current. Smoke particles disrupt this current, triggering the alarm. Because the alpha source is sealed inside the detector and alpha particles cannot penetrate the casing, the risk to the user is negligible — a clear example where the benefit (early warning of fires) substantially outweighs the risk.

Risk–Benefit Reasoning in Practice

Good risk–benefit reasoning requires thinking about the specific context, not just listing generic risks and benefits. For a given scenario, consider:

• Who is exposed? A 70-year-old patient with cancer faces a very different calculus from a healthy 20-year-old having an elective scan.
• What is the dose? Background radiation is always present; a procedure that adds a small fraction to this carries less additional risk than one that significantly increases total exposure.
• What is the alternative? If refusing a scan means a treatable cancer goes undetected, the risk of the scan is almost certainly worth taking.
• What is the uncertainty? At very low doses, cancer risk is hard to measure precisely because the effect is too small to detect against background rates. This uncertainty cuts both ways — it does not mean the risk is zero or that it is large.

Extended-response questions expect you to evaluate a named scenario using this kind of reasoning — not just to list facts about radiation types.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 6-mark questions on radiation risk and benefit, the mark scheme rewards evaluation: you must identify the specific benefit in the given scenario (what the radiation does and why it helps), identify the specific risk (which type of radiation, which cells are at risk and why), then reach a justified conclusion. Simply listing “benefits: cures cancer; risks: causes cancer” will not score highly — you need to explain the science behind each point and weigh them against each other. The ‘Suggest’ command word means you should apply the science to the context given in the question, not just recall general facts.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ionising radiation (alpha, beta, gamma, X-rays) carries enough energy to damage DNA and living cells; the risk depends on dose, duration of exposure, type of radiation and whether the source is internal (contamination) or external (irradiation).
  • Medical uses include X-ray imaging, radiotherapy, radioactive tracers (gamma-emitting isotopes with short half-lives) and sterilisation — each exploits radiation’s penetrating or ionising properties.
  • Every radiation use involves weighing benefits against risks in context: the dose, who is exposed, what the alternative is, and what is genuinely uncertain all matter.

lessons.title: Climate Change: A Physics Perspective
lessons.description: How EM radiation, Earth's energy balance and human emissions interact to warm the planet.
lessons.content_html:
Two Lessons, Two Disciplines

Climate change appears in two different parts of your course — once in chemistry (about the chemical composition of the atmosphere and the evidence for rising CO₂ from human activities) and once here in physics. The physics angle focuses on how radiation and energy balance explain why CO₂ traps heat. Understanding both together gives you the most complete picture and the tools to answer questions from either discipline.

Earth’s Radiation Balance

The Earth receives energy from the Sun as shortwave radiation — predominantly visible light and some UV. It also loses energy by emitting its own longwave radiation (infrared). For the climate to be stable, the energy arriving must equal the energy leaving. This balance is called the energy balance.

Not all the solar radiation that arrives at Earth’s surface is absorbed. Some is reflected back to space. The fraction of incoming radiation that is reflected is called the albedo. Surfaces with high albedo (ice, snow, clouds) reflect more solar energy and absorb less. Surfaces with low albedo (dark ocean, forests) absorb more. The average albedo of Earth is roughly 0.3, meaning about 30% of incoming solar energy is reflected without heating the planet.

Key Fact

High albedo surfaces (ice, snow, clouds) reflect solar radiation; low albedo surfaces (ocean, forest) absorb it. As Arctic ice melts, it is replaced by darker ocean water — lower albedo means more absorption and more warming. This is a positive feedback loop.

The Greenhouse Effect

Earth’s surface warms because it absorbs solar radiation and re-emits this energy as infrared radiation. The atmosphere contains gases — principally water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane — that absorb this outgoing infrared and re-emit some of it back towards Earth’s surface. These are called greenhouse gases. Without them, Earth’s average surface temperature would be far colder than it is — the greenhouse effect is natural and essential to life.

The problem is not the greenhouse effect itself but its enhancement. As human activities release more CO₂ and methane into the atmosphere, more infrared is absorbed and returned to the surface. The energy balance is disrupted: more energy arrives at the surface than leaves to space, and the planet warms until a new equilibrium is reached at a higher temperature.

A molecule absorbs radiation when the energy of the photon matches a vibrational mode of the molecule. CO₂ and H₂O have molecular structures with vibrational modes (bending and stretching of bonds) that correspond to infrared wavelengths. Nitrogen (N₂) and oxygen (O₂), which make up most of the atmosphere, are symmetrical diatomic molecules with no such vibrational modes at infrared wavelengths — they are essentially transparent to outgoing infrared. This is why a small increase in CO₂ concentration has a disproportionately large effect on the greenhouse effect: the main atmospheric gases already let infrared through; adding CO₂ closes the gaps.

Key Fact

Earth’s surface emits infrared. Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₂ = methane, water vapour) absorb this infrared and re-emit some back to the surface. More greenhouse gas → more infrared returned → higher equilibrium surface temperature.

The Electromagnetic Spectrum and Climate

Understanding why the atmosphere behaves differently towards incoming and outgoing radiation requires placing both on the electromagnetic spectrum. Incoming solar radiation peaks in the visible and near-infrared region (short wavelengths). Earth, at its surface temperature, emits radiation that peaks in the mid-infrared region (longer wavelengths). The atmosphere is largely transparent to the incoming shortwave radiation but absorbs strongly in specific infrared wavelength bands — precisely where greenhouse gases have their vibrational modes.

UV radiation from the Sun is mostly absorbed by ozone in the stratosphere before reaching the surface. Visible light passes through the atmosphere largely unaffected. The key action is at the infrared end: shortwave in, longwave out, with the greenhouse gases acting as an asymmetric filter.

Climate scientists use computer models to predict how rising greenhouse gas concentrations will affect global temperatures. These models are built on well-established physics (the radiation balance principles covered in this lesson) and tested against historical climate data. Where models from different research groups using different assumptions agree, scientists have greater confidence in the prediction. Where they disagree, this signals genuine uncertainty about feedbacks and timescales.

The key evidence that the current warming is human-caused rather than natural includes: the rate of warming is faster than any natural cycle detected in ice-core records; rising CO₂ concentrations in the atmosphere correlate with industrial activity; the isotopic signature of atmospheric CO₂ shows it comes from burning fossil fuels; and the stratosphere is cooling while the troposphere warms — the pattern expected from greenhouse gas forcing, not from increased solar output. This is an example of how multiple independent lines of evidence converge to support one explanation — a hallmark of strong scientific reasoning.

Consequences and the Need for Action

A disrupted energy balance has physical consequences that flow directly from the physics. Warmer oceans expand (thermal expansion) and melt land ice, raising sea levels. Warmer air holds more water vapour, intensifying rainfall events and droughts. The extra energy in the climate system drives more intense weather. These effects are not uniform globally, but the physics of the energy imbalance means they are unavoidable until the atmosphere returns to a new equilibrium.

Reducing greenhouse gas emissions directly addresses the physical cause: fewer greenhouse gas molecules in the atmosphere means less infrared is absorbed and returned to the surface, allowing the energy balance to stabilise at a lower equilibrium temperature. Switching from fossil fuels to renewable energy sources reduces the rate at which CO₂ is added to the atmosphere without removing CO₂ already there — hence why scientists also discuss carbon capture technologies that directly reduce atmospheric CO₂ concentrations.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on climate change physics expect you to use precise scientific language: write “infrared radiation” not just “heat”; write “greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared” not just “CO₂ traps heat”. For 6-mark questions, show that you understand the physical mechanism (energy balance, infrared absorption) AND can evaluate evidence or consequences. Avoid vague phrases like “pollution damages the atmosphere” — be specific about which radiation, which gases, and which physical process. For ‘Suggest’ questions about climate models, remember that uncertainty in predictions does not mean the science is wrong — explain what uncertainty means in a scientific context.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Earth’s energy balance: shortwave solar radiation in, longwave infrared radiation out. Albedo determines how much solar energy is reflected; high-albedo surfaces (ice, snow) reflect more and absorb less.
  • Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₂, water vapour) absorb outgoing infrared and re-emit some back to the surface; more greenhouse gas disrupts the energy balance and raises equilibrium surface temperature.
  • The atmosphere is largely transparent to incoming shortwave (visible) radiation but absorbs strongly at infrared wavelengths where greenhouse gases have vibrational modes — this asymmetry is the physical basis of the greenhouse effect.

lessons.title: Wave Behaviour and the EM Spectrum
lessons.description: Transverse and longitudinal waves, the equation v = fλ, and the EM spectrum of uses and hazards.
lessons.content_html:
What Is a Wave?

Waves transfer energy from one place to another without transferring matter. The particles of the medium vibrate about their rest positions but do not travel along with the wave — it is the disturbance that moves, not the material. This is why you can feel a sound wave in your chest even though no air travels from the speaker to you; instead, the air molecules pass the vibration along like a row of falling dominoes.

All waves fall into one of two categories. In transverse waves, the vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer — the wave forms crests and troughs. Examples include light, water surface ripples and all electromagnetic waves. In longitudinal waves, the vibrations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer. Instead of crests and troughs, longitudinal waves have compressions (regions where particles are pressed together) and rarefactions (regions where particles spread apart). Sound is the main longitudinal wave at GCSE.

Key Fact

Transverse waves: vibrations perpendicular to direction of travel — light, water ripples, all EM waves. Longitudinal waves: vibrations parallel to direction of travel — sound. Only longitudinal waves have compressions and rarefactions.

Wave Properties

All waves share four measurable properties:

• Amplitude — the maximum displacement from rest position, measured in metres. A larger amplitude means more energy. For sound, greater amplitude means a louder sound; for light, it means brighter light.
• Wavelength (\(\lambda\)) — the distance from one crest (or compression) to the next. Measured in metres.
• Frequency (\(f\)) — the number of complete waves passing a fixed point per second, measured in hertz (Hz). For sound, higher frequency means higher pitch.
• Period (\(T\)) — the time for one complete wave to pass a point. Period and frequency are reciprocals: \(T = \frac{1}{f}\).

The Wave Speed Equation

The relationship between wave speed, frequency and wavelength is one of the most important equations in physics:

$$v = f \times \lambda$$

Where \(v\) is wave speed in m/s, \(f\) is frequency in Hz, and \(\lambda\) is wavelength in m. This equation applies to all waves — whether a ripple on a pond or a gamma ray from a radioactive source. You can rearrange it to find frequency (\(f = \frac{v}{\lambda}\)) or wavelength (\(\lambda = \frac{v}{f}\)).

Q1: A sound wave has a frequency of 440 Hz and travels at 340 m/s in air. Calculate its wavelength.

\(\lambda = \frac{v}{f} = \frac{340}{440} = 0.77 \text{ m}\) (to 2 s.f.)

Q2: A radio wave has a wavelength of 1.5 m. The speed of radio waves in air is approximately \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s. Calculate the frequency.

\(f = \frac{v}{\lambda} = \frac{3 \times 10^8}{1.5} = 2 \times 10^8 \text{ Hz} = 200 \text{ MHz}\)

Reflection, Refraction and Diffraction

Waves can interact with boundaries and obstacles in three important ways:

• Reflection — a wave bounces off a surface. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (both measured from the normal — an imaginary line perpendicular to the surface). Speed, frequency and wavelength are unchanged.
• Refraction — a wave changes speed when passing from one medium to another (e.g. light entering glass from air). If it hits the boundary at an angle, it also changes direction. A wave bends towards the normal when it slows down (entering a denser medium). Frequency stays the same; wavelength and speed change.
• Diffraction — a wave spreads out as it passes through a gap or around an obstacle. The spreading is greatest when the gap size is similar to the wavelength. This is why sound diffracts around a doorway (sound wavelengths are comparable to door sizes) but light does not (visible light wavelengths are millions of times shorter than a doorway).

Key Fact

Reflection: speed, frequency and wavelength all unchanged — wave bounces off at the same angle it hit. Refraction: speed and wavelength change; frequency does NOT change. Diffraction: greatest spreading when gap width is similar to wavelength.

The Electromagnetic Spectrum

All electromagnetic waves are transverse waves that travel at the same speed in a vacuum: approximately \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s (the speed of light). They are arranged on the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing frequency (and decreasing wavelength):

Radio waves → microwaves → infrared → visible light → ultraviolet → X-rays → gamma rays

As frequency increases, wavelength decreases (since \(v = f\lambda\) and \(v\) is constant). Higher-frequency (shorter-wavelength) EM radiation generally carries more energy per photon and tends to be more ionising — which is why UV, X-rays and gamma rays are more hazardous to living tissue than radio waves or infrared.

Radio waves: broadcasting (TV, radio), satellite communication. Very low energy; not hazardous in normal use.
Microwaves: mobile phone signals, satellite data, cooking (microwave ovens heat water molecules). May cause tissue heating at high intensities.
Infrared: remote controls, thermal imaging, optical fibre communication, radiant heaters. Causes skin burns at high intensities.
Visible light: human vision, photography, optical fibre communication. Safe at normal intensities.
Ultraviolet (UV): causes skin tanning and can cause skin cancer and eye damage; used in fluorescent lights and sterilising water. Ionising at high frequency end.
X-rays: medical imaging, airport security scanners. Ionising — can damage DNA; doses kept as low as reasonably practicable in medical use.
Gamma rays: radiotherapy (killing cancer cells), sterilisation, medical tracers. Ionising — can cause cancer; penetrating power makes them both useful and hazardous.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For wave calculations, always state the equation you are using and substitute values with units before working out the answer. The most common error is confusing frequency and wavelength when substituting into \(v = f\lambda\). Check your answer makes sense: the frequency of visible light is around \(10^{14}\) Hz — if your answer for a visible light frequency is 400 Hz you know something has gone wrong. For the EM spectrum, you need to know the order, typical uses and the hazards linked to each region. ‘Explain’ questions expect you to link a property (high energy, ionising, penetrating) to the observed effect (causes cancer, kills bacteria, passes through bone).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Transverse waves (vibrations perpendicular to travel — light, all EM waves) differ from longitudinal waves (vibrations parallel to travel — sound). Wave speed is given by \(v = f\lambda\).
  • Reflection: wave bounces, speed/frequency/wavelength unchanged. Refraction: wave changes speed and direction, frequency unchanged. Diffraction: wave spreads, greatest when gap ≈ wavelength.
  • All EM waves travel at \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s in a vacuum. Higher frequency = shorter wavelength = more energy per photon. UV, X-rays and gamma rays are ionising; radio, microwave and infrared are not.

lessons.title: Energy Resources and Demand
lessons.description: Where our energy comes from, how it is used, and why demand keeps changing.
lessons.content_html:
Where Does Our Energy Come From?

Every time you switch on a light or charge a phone, you are drawing on an energy source somewhere in the national supply chain. The main energy sources available to us fall into two categories:

• Non-renewable sources will eventually run out. They include fossil fuels (coal, oil and natural gas, formed over millions of years from dead organic material) and nuclear fuel (uranium and plutonium). Fossil fuels currently provide the majority of global energy, but their reserves are finite and their combustion releases carbon dioxide, contributing to climate change.
• Renewable sources are naturally replenished. They include solar, wind, hydroelectric, tidal, geothermal, wave and biomass.

Key Fact

Non-renewable: fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) and nuclear. Renewable: solar, wind, hydroelectric, tidal, geothermal, wave, biomass. Nuclear is non-renewable (uses uranium ore) but produces no direct CO₂ emissions during operation.

Energy Demand and How It Changes

Energy demand is not constant. It varies over daily, seasonal and historical timescales:

• Daily variation: demand is highest in the morning (when people wake and use appliances) and in the early evening (cooking, lighting). It falls overnight. Power grid operators must match supply to demand in real time.
• Seasonal variation: demand is higher in winter because of heating and lighting needs.
• Long-term trends: energy demand has grown historically as populations increase and living standards rise. However, improvements in energy efficiency (better insulation, LED lighting, efficient appliances) are beginning to reduce the energy needed per unit of economic output in many countries.

The concept of baseload is important: some power stations (typically nuclear and large gas plants) run continuously to provide a steady minimum supply. Peak demand capacity is additional supply brought in when demand surges above this minimum.

Environmental Impacts

Every energy source has environmental trade-offs. The choice of energy mix involves balancing cost, reliability, environmental impact and carbon emissions:

Solar: no CO₂ during operation, low running costs. Disadvantages: only generates in daylight and sunshine; large land area needed for solar farms; high upfront cost.
Wind: no CO₂ during operation, abundant resource. Disadvantages: intermittent — only generates when wind blows; visual and noise impact; can harm birds.
Hydroelectric: very reliable, can respond instantly to demand changes. Disadvantages: requires damming rivers, flooding valleys, displacing communities and disrupting ecosystems.
Tidal: highly predictable (tides are regular). Disadvantages: very expensive to build; limited suitable locations; can affect marine ecosystems.
Geothermal: reliable, low emissions, continuous output. Disadvantages: only available where hot rocks are near the surface (volcanic regions); high drilling costs.
Biomass: considered broadly carbon-neutral if managed sustainably (CO₂ released equals CO₂ absorbed during crop growth). Disadvantages: requires large areas of land; produces air pollution when burned; carbon neutrality is disputed if land use change is factored in.

Fossil fuels release CO₂ and other pollutants when burned. Nuclear power produces no CO₂ during generation but creates radioactive waste that must be stored safely for very long periods. On a full lifecycle analysis (which includes the energy and emissions from manufacturing, construction and decommissioning), wind, solar and nuclear all have much lower carbon footprints than coal or gas.

Key Fact

No energy source is without trade-offs. Renewables produce little CO₂ during operation but many are intermittent or require specific geography. Fossil fuels are reliable and energy-dense but emit greenhouse gases. Nuclear is reliable and low-carbon but produces long-lived radioactive waste.

Sankey Diagrams and Energy Transfer

A Sankey diagram shows how energy flows through a system. The total width of the arrow on the left (input energy) equals the total of all arrows on the right (useful output + wasted energy). This reflects the principle of conservation of energy — energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred.

A coal power station takes in 100 J of chemical energy in fuel. Of this, 35 J is transferred as useful electrical energy and 65 J is wasted as heat (to the cooling towers and surroundings). On a Sankey diagram, the input arrow is 100 units wide. The useful output arrow pointing right is 35 units wide. The wasted heat arrow pointing down is 65 units wide. The total width of outputs (35 + 65) equals the input (100).

The efficiency of this transfer is:

$$\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful energy output}}{\text{total energy input}} \times 100\%$$

$$= \frac{35}{100} \times 100\% = 35\%$$

The remaining 65% is dissipated as thermal energy to the surroundings, where it is no longer in a useful form. This is not energy being ‘lost’ — it still exists — but it has been transferred to a form that is too spread out to be useful.

The National Grid

The National Grid is the network of high-voltage cables and transformers that distributes electricity across the country. Electricity is transmitted at high voltage to minimise energy losses during transmission. Because power loss in cables is proportional to the square of the current (\(P = I^2 R\)), reducing the current by using a higher voltage substantially reduces wasted heat in the wires.

Step-up transformers at power stations increase the voltage (to hundreds of thousands of volts) for efficient long-distance transmission. Step-down transformers near homes and businesses reduce the voltage to safe levels for use (230 V in UK homes). Balancing supply and demand on the grid in real time requires careful management as more intermittent renewable sources connect to the system.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For Sankey diagrams, always check that your widths add up: input = useful output + wasted output. Efficiency calculations use the equation \(\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output}}{\text{total input}} \times 100\%\). For evaluation questions about energy sources, give a named example for each claim — do not just write ‘it pollutes the environment’; write ‘burning coal releases CO₂, which is a greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change’. The ‘Suggest’ command word means you should apply the principles in the question to a context you have not necessarily seen before — use the science, not a memorised answer.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Non-renewable sources (fossil fuels, nuclear) will run out; renewables (solar, wind, hydro, tidal, geothermal, wave, biomass) are replenished naturally. No source is without trade-offs between cost, reliability and environmental impact.
  • Energy demand varies daily (peak in morning and evening), seasonally (higher in winter) and historically. Baseload power runs continuously; peak capacity responds to surges in demand.
  • Sankey diagrams show energy flow (width proportional to energy); efficiency = useful output ÷ total input × 100%. The National Grid transmits at high voltage to reduce current and minimise wasted energy in cables.

lessons.title: Generating Electricity
lessons.description: How turbines and generators make electricity, and how the National Grid delivers it to your home.
lessons.content_html:
From Fuel to Electricity

When you boil your kettle, the electricity that heats the element began its journey kilometres away — perhaps in a wind farm on a hillside, or inside a large power station. Understanding how it got there involves two key ideas: the generator and the National Grid.

In most power stations, fuel (such as natural gas, coal, nuclear fuel, or the heat from geothermal sources) is used to produce steam. The steam pushes against the blades of a turbine, making it spin at high speed. The spinning turbine is connected to a generator, which converts the rotational energy into electrical energy. In a wind turbine, the wind itself turns the blades directly — no steam is needed.

A generator works by electromagnetic induction: when a coil of wire rotates inside a magnetic field (or when a magnet rotates inside a coil), a changing magnetic field induces a potential difference and drives a current. The output is alternating current (AC) because as the coil spins, the direction of the induced current reverses every half turn. The UK mains supply is AC at a frequency of 50 Hz and a voltage of about 230 V.

Key Fact

In most power stations: fuel heats water → steam turns a turbine → turbine drives a generator → generator produces AC electricity. Wind turbines skip the steam stage. Generators work by electromagnetic induction.

Transformers and Voltage

Once electricity leaves the generator, its voltage must be changed before it travels long distances. A transformer uses electromagnetic induction in an iron core to increase or decrease voltage. There are two types in the National Grid system:

• A step-up transformer at the power station increases the voltage to very high levels (typically hundreds of thousands of volts) before electricity enters the transmission cables. At higher voltage, the current is lower.
• A step-down transformer at a local substation reduces the voltage back to 230 V for safe use in homes and small businesses.

Transformers only work with AC — they rely on a changing magnetic field in the iron core to induce a voltage in the secondary coil. DC produces a constant (non-changing) field and would not induce any current. This is one of the main reasons the National Grid uses AC rather than DC.

The turns ratio of a transformer determines how it changes voltage. For an ideal (100% efficient) transformer:

$$\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{N_p}{N_s}$$

Where \(V_p\) is the primary voltage, \(V_s\) is the secondary voltage, \(N_p\) is the number of turns on the primary coil, and \(N_s\) is the number of turns on the secondary coil. If the secondary coil has more turns than the primary, the voltage is stepped up; if it has fewer turns, the voltage is stepped down. Because power is conserved in an ideal transformer (\(V_p \times I_p = V_s \times I_s\)), a step-up in voltage is always accompanied by a step-down in current — and vice versa.

Why Transmit at High Voltage?

The cables in the National Grid have resistance. Any current flowing through resistance causes energy to be wasted as heat: \(P_{\text{loss}} = I^2 \times R\). Because current is squared in this equation, even a small reduction in current makes a dramatic difference to energy losses.

By stepping voltage up before transmission, current is reduced proportionally (since power = voltage × current, and power must stay the same). Lower current means far less heat is produced in the cables. This is why transmission losses in the National Grid are small — the grid is a highly efficient system even though the cables themselves stretch for thousands of kilometres across the country.

Key Fact

Transmitting at high voltage reduces current. Since cable heat loss = \(I^2R\), low current means very little energy is wasted. Step-up transformers make the grid efficient; step-down transformers make it safe for homes.

The National Grid in Practice

The National Grid is the system that connects electricity producers to consumers across the country. Electricity enters the grid at high voltage from a range of sources — large thermal power stations, offshore wind farms, solar farms, and others. It travels along overhead power lines (on tall pylons) or underground cables.

At substations, step-down transformers reduce the voltage in stages. Industrial users may draw electricity at an intermediate voltage (e.g. 11,000 V), while homes and shops receive it at 230 V. The Grid is a national system, so electricity generated in one part of the country can be directed to areas of high demand elsewhere. This makes the supply more reliable and responsive to peaks in demand (such as during half-time of a major televised sporting event, when millions of people simultaneously use kettles).

Question: A power station outputs 500 kW. If transmitted at 250 V the current is 2000 A; if transmitted at 25,000 V the current is 20 A. The cable has a resistance of 4 Ω. Calculate the power lost as heat in each case.

At 250 V: \(P_{\text{loss}} = I^2 \times R = 2000^2 \times 4 = 16{,}000{,}000 \text{ W} = 16 \text{ MW}\). This is more than the station’s output — completely impractical.
At 25,000 V: \(P_{\text{loss}} = 20^2 \times 4 = 1600 \text{ W} = 1.6 \text{ kW}\). Less than 0.4% of the power is wasted — far more efficient.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For ‘Explain’ questions on the National Grid, always link the physics: high voltage → low current → less heat loss (\(P = I^2R\)). Don’t just state “high voltage reduces energy loss” — examiners want the causal chain with the equation. For ‘Suggest’ questions about a novel generation scenario, identify the energy transfer steps and check whether a transformer is needed and why. Remember: transformers only work with AC.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Most power stations convert fuel energy to steam, which drives a turbine, which drives a generator that produces AC electricity via electromagnetic induction. Wind turbines spin generators directly.
  • Step-up transformers increase voltage (and reduce current) for long-distance transmission; step-down transformers reduce voltage to safe domestic levels. Transformers only work with AC.
  • High-voltage transmission keeps current low, minimising heat lost in cables (since \(P_{\text{loss}} = I^2R\)), making the National Grid efficient.

lessons.title: Current, Voltage and Resistance
lessons.description: What current really is, what determines it, and why resistance matters in real circuits.
lessons.content_html:
Charge and Current

Current is the rate at which electric charge flows through a conductor. In metal wires, the charge carriers are free electrons — electrons that are not bound to any particular atom and can drift through the material when a potential difference is applied. For current to flow, two conditions must be met: there must be a potential difference driving the charge, and the circuit must form a complete closed loop with no gaps.

The equation linking charge, current and time is:

$$Q = I \times t$$

Where \(Q\) is charge (coulombs, C), \(I\) is current (amperes, A), and \(t\) is time (seconds, s). One ampere means one coulomb of charge passes a point every second. Current is measured using an ammeter connected in series. Potential difference is measured using a voltmeter connected in parallel across the component.

Key Fact

Current is measured in amperes (A), potential difference in volts (V). Current is NOT ‘used up’ by components — charge flows continuously around a closed circuit. Energy is transferred from the charge carriers, not the current itself.

Resistance and Ohm’s Law

Resistance opposes the flow of current. The greater a component’s resistance, the smaller the current that flows for a given potential difference. The relationship between these three quantities is:

$$V = I \times R$$

Where \(V\) is potential difference (V), \(I\) is current (A), and \(R\) is resistance (\(\Omega\)). This can be rearranged: \(I = \frac{V}{R}\) or \(R = \frac{V}{I}\). Ohm’s Law is a special case of this: it states that the current is directly proportional to the potential difference only if the temperature does not change. Components that obey this are called ohmic conductors.

Question: A resistor has a potential difference of 12 V across it and a current of 0.4 A flowing through it. Calculate its resistance.

Answer: \(R = \frac{V}{I} = \frac{12}{0.4} = 30 \, \Omega\). Note: current in amps, voltage in volts, resistance in ohms. Always write the equation, substitute, then calculate.

I–V Characteristics

An I–V characteristic graph shows how current varies with potential difference. You need to know the shapes for three key components:

• Ohmic resistor: a straight line through the origin. The gradient is constant, showing that resistance does not change. This confirms Ohm’s law.
• Filament lamp: a curve that starts steep and flattens at higher voltages. As more current flows, the filament heats up, increasing its resistance. The curve is symmetrical in both directions.
• Diode: current only flows in the forward direction. In reverse, resistance is extremely high and effectively no current flows. There is a threshold voltage (around 0.6 V for silicon diodes) below which forward current is also negligible.

Key Fact

Ohmic resistor: straight line (constant resistance). Filament lamp: curve (resistance increases with temperature). Diode: current only in one direction (very high reverse resistance).

Series and Parallel Circuits

In a series circuit, all components are in a single loop. The same current flows through every component. Potential difference is shared — the voltages across components add up to the supply voltage. Total resistance is the sum of individual resistances: \(R_{\text{total}} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3\). If any component breaks, the whole circuit stops.

In a parallel circuit, components are on separate branches. Potential difference is the same across every branch (and equal to the supply voltage). Current splits between branches — more current takes the lower-resistance path. Adding resistors in parallel decreases total resistance because there are more paths for charge to flow. If one branch breaks, others continue to work. Household wiring is parallel so that each appliance receives the full 230 V and can be switched independently.

Some components have resistance that responds to environmental conditions:

• A light-dependent resistor (LDR) has high resistance in the dark and low resistance in bright light. It is used in automatic streetlights and security systems.
• An NTC thermistor (negative temperature coefficient) has high resistance when cold and low resistance when hot. It is used in temperature sensors, fire alarms and thermostat circuits.

Both devices are non-ohmic — their resistance changes with conditions, so the current through them is not simply proportional to voltage. They are often used in potential divider circuits to give a variable voltage output.

Series: Two resistors, 6 Ω and 4 Ω, connected in series to a 10 V supply. \(R_{\text{total}} = 6 + 4 = 10 \, \Omega\). \(I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{10}{10} = 1 \text{ A}\) (same through both).

Parallel (same resistors): Voltage across each branch = 10 V. Current through 6 Ω branch: \(I_1 = \frac{10}{6} \approx 1.67 \text{ A}\). Current through 4 Ω branch: \(I_2 = \frac{10}{4} = 2.5 \text{ A}\). Total current from supply = \(1.67 + 2.5 = 4.17 \text{ A}\) — more than in series, because parallel reduces total resistance.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For ‘Explain’ questions on I–V characteristics, always link the shape of the graph to what happens to resistance — don’t just describe the shape. The most common error is confusing current and potential difference units: current is always measured in amperes (A) and potential difference in volts (V). On a ‘Suggest’ question about a novel circuit, identify whether components are in series or parallel and apply the relevant rules for current and voltage distribution.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Current (A) is the rate of flow of charge; potential difference (V) drives it; resistance (Ω) opposes it. Ohm’s law (V = IR) links all three — but only for ohmic conductors at constant temperature.
  • In series circuits, current is the same everywhere and voltages add up. In parallel circuits, voltage is the same across every branch and currents add up. Adding resistors in parallel reduces total resistance.
  • I–V graphs reveal how resistance changes: a straight line means constant resistance (ohmic), a curve means resistance increases with temperature (filament lamp), and a one-way graph means a diode.

lessons.title: Power, Energy Transfer and Bills
lessons.description: How appliances transfer energy, what efficiency means, and how your electricity bill is calculated.
lessons.content_html:
Electrical Power

Every electrical appliance transfers energy. The rate at which it does so is its power. A 100 W bulb transfers 100 joules of energy every second; a 3 kW kettle transfers 3,000 joules every second. The key equations for electrical power are:

$$P = V \times I$$

$$P = I^2 \times R$$

Where \(P\) is power (W), \(V\) is potential difference (V), \(I\) is current (A), and \(R\) is resistance (\(\Omega\)). The second equation comes from substituting \(V = IR\) into the first. It is useful when you know current and resistance but not voltage.

Key Fact

Power: \(P = VI\) and \(P = I^2R\). Both give power in watts (W). Use the first when you know voltage and current; use the second when you know current and resistance.

Energy Transferred

The total energy transferred by an appliance depends on its power and the time it runs:

$$E = P \times t$$

Where \(E\) is energy (J), \(P\) is power (W), and \(t\) is time (s). Energy can also be calculated using the charge that flows: \(E = Q \times V\), where \(Q\) is charge (C) and \(V\) is potential difference (V). This tells you how much energy is transferred to each coulomb of charge as it passes through the component.

For domestic electricity bills, energy is measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh) rather than joules, because joules are impractically small for household use. To calculate energy in kWh: multiply power in kilowatts by time in hours. The cost is then: \(\text{cost} = \text{energy (kWh)} \times \text{price per kWh}\).

Scenario: A household uses the following appliances on one day: a 3 kW electric shower for 0.25 hours, a 2 kW oven for 1.5 hours, and a 0.1 kW television for 4 hours. Electricity costs 28p per kWh. Calculate the total daily cost.

Step 1 — Energy used by each:
Shower: \(3 \times 0.25 = 0.75 \text{ kWh}\)
Oven: \(2 \times 1.5 = 3.0 \text{ kWh}\)
TV: \(0.1 \times 4 = 0.4 \text{ kWh}\)
Step 2 — Total energy: \(0.75 + 3.0 + 0.4 = 4.15 \text{ kWh}\)
Step 3 — Cost: \(4.15 \times 28\text{p} = 116.2\text{p} \approx \text{£1.16}\)

AC, DC and Mains Wiring

Direct current (DC) flows in one direction only. Alternating current (AC) constantly reverses direction. The UK mains supply is AC at approximately 230 V and a frequency of 50 Hz. AC is used for the mains because its voltage can be easily changed using transformers, which is essential for the National Grid.

A UK three-pin plug has three wires with specific colours and roles:

• Live (brown) — carries the AC supply at about 230 V. Always dangerous, even when a switch is open.
• Neutral (blue) — completes the circuit; normally at 0 V.
• Earth (green and yellow) — a safety wire connected to metal casings; provides a low-resistance path to earth if a fault occurs.

A fuse is always connected in the live wire. If current exceeds the fuse rating, the fuse wire melts and breaks the circuit. The residual current device (RCD) provides even faster protection by detecting tiny current imbalances.

Key Fact

UK plug wires: live (brown) at 230 V, neutral (blue) at 0 V, earth (green & yellow) for safety. The fuse is in the live wire and melts if current is too high. The earth wire prevents the casing becoming dangerously live.

Efficiency

Efficiency measures how well a device converts input energy into useful output energy. The equation is:

$$\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful power output}}{\text{total power input}}$$

Efficiency can be expressed as a decimal or multiplied by 100 to give a percentage. An incandescent light bulb might be only 5% efficient — 95% of electrical energy is wasted as heat rather than light. An LED lamp doing the same lighting job might be around 60-80% efficient, which is why the switch to LED lighting has been a significant energy-saving measure. No device is 100% efficient; energy is always lost to the surroundings, usually as heat.

Question: An electric motor has an input power of 800 W. It does useful mechanical work at a rate of 600 W. Calculate its efficiency and state what happens to the remaining 200 W.

Answer: \(\text{efficiency} = \frac{600}{800} = 0.75\) (or 75%). The remaining 200 W (25%) is transferred to the surroundings as heat due to friction in the bearings and resistance in the motor windings. This energy is not useful — it dissipates into the environment and cannot be recovered.

Reducing Energy Use at Home

Understanding power and efficiency helps households make informed decisions about energy use. The biggest energy consumers in a typical home are heating and hot water (including showers and washing machines), followed by cooking, then refrigeration and lighting. Identifying which appliances draw the most power — and for how long — is the first step in reducing energy bills and environmental impact.

For any given task, a more efficient appliance transfers more of the input electrical energy to a useful output. Replacing a 60 W incandescent bulb with an 8 W LED that produces the same brightness reduces the power draw by over 85%. Over hundreds of hours of use, this saving accumulates significantly on an electricity bill. Energy ratings on appliances (from A to G in the UK, with A being most efficient) allow consumers to compare efficiency at the point of purchase. A highly efficient appliance costs more upfront but typically pays back the extra cost through lower running costs over its lifetime.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For ‘Suggest’ questions about energy costs, always convert power to kilowatts and time to hours before multiplying — then multiply by the unit price. For efficiency questions, identify which output is “useful” first. A common error is treating all output as useful. On extended-response questions about domestic electricity, link physics (P = VI, efficiency) to real contexts such as choosing appliances or reducing bills.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Electrical power (W) = VI = I2R. Energy transferred (J) = power × time. For bills, use kilowatts and hours: energy in kWh = kW × hours; cost = kWh × price per unit.
  • UK mains supply is AC at 230 V, 50 Hz. The live (brown) wire is dangerous; the fuse is always in the live wire; the earth (green & yellow) wire prevents metal casings becoming live.
  • Efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input. No device is 100% efficient — energy is always lost as heat. Higher efficiency means less energy wasted for the same useful output.

lessons.title: Magnetic Fields and Electric Motors
lessons.description: Permanent and induced magnets, electromagnets, the motor effect, and Fleming's left-hand rule.
lessons.content_html:
Permanent and Induced Magnets

A permanent magnet produces a magnetic field continuously. It always has a north pole and a south pole, and the fundamental rule of magnetism applies: like poles repel; unlike poles attract. Common permanent magnet materials include iron, steel, nickel and cobalt — these are all magnetic materials.

An induced magnet is different — it only becomes magnetic when placed inside another magnet’s field. The induced poles arrange themselves so that unlike poles face the permanent magnet, meaning an induced magnet is always attracted to the magnet that induces it. This explains why an ordinary iron nail is picked up by a permanent magnet even though the nail itself is not a magnet.

Key Fact

Like poles repel; unlike poles attract. An induced magnet is temporary — it only has magnetism while inside another magnet’s field — and always attracts the permanent magnet that induced it.

Magnetic Fields

A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where magnetic forces act. Fields are represented by field lines:

• Field lines run from north to south outside the magnet.
• Where lines are closer together, the field is stronger.
• The field is strongest at the poles and weakens with distance.
• Field lines never cross.

You can map magnetic fields using a plotting compass: place it near the magnet, mark where the needle points, move the compass to the new position, and repeat. Connecting the marks gives smooth field lines. Iron filings also show the pattern visually as they align along field lines. The Earth itself has a magnetic field, produced by convection currents in its liquid outer core — this is why a compass needle points roughly north.

When current flows through a straight wire, it creates a circular magnetic field around the wire. A solenoid is a coil of wire — the fields from each turn combine to produce a strong, uniform field inside the coil with clear north and south poles at each end.

Adding a soft iron core inside the solenoid creates an electromagnet. The iron core becomes an induced magnet and dramatically strengthens the field. Unlike permanent magnets, electromagnets can be switched on and off and their strength adjusted by changing the current, the number of coil turns, or the core material. Uses include scrapyard cranes, electric bells, relays, loudspeakers and MRI scanners.

The Motor Effect

When a current-carrying conductor is placed inside a magnetic field, it experiences a force. This is called the motor effect. The force is greatest when the conductor is at right angles to the field and zero when it is parallel to the field.

The force can be increased by:

• Increasing the current through the conductor
• Increasing the magnetic flux density (using a stronger magnet)
• Increasing the length of conductor within the field

These relationships are captured in the equation:

$$F = B \times I \times l$$

Where \(F\) is force (N), \(B\) is magnetic flux density (T), \(I\) is current (A), and \(l\) is the length of the conductor in the field (m).

Key Fact

The motor effect equation: \(F = BIl\). Force is greatest when conductor and field are at right angles. Increasing current, field strength, or conductor length all increase the force.

Fleming’s Left-Hand Rule

Fleming’s left-hand rule tells you the direction of the force. Hold your left hand with the thumb, first finger and second finger all at right angles to each other:

• Thumb (thuMb) = Motion / force direction
• First finger (First) = Field direction (north to south)
• Second finger (seCond) = Current direction (conventional, from positive to negative)

If any one of the three quantities reverses (e.g. the current direction reverses, or you flip the magnet so field reverses), the force direction also reverses.

In a simple DC electric motor, a current-carrying coil sits between two permanent magnets. Using Fleming’s left-hand rule, the two sides of the coil experience forces in opposite directions (because current flows in opposite directions on each side), creating a turning effect (torque) that spins the coil.

Without further modification, the coil would stop after rotating halfway. A split-ring commutator reverses the current direction every half turn, ensuring the forces always produce rotation in the same direction — giving continuous spinning. Motor speed can be increased by using a stronger magnetic field, a larger current, or more coil turns.

Real-World Applications of Electromagnetism

The motor effect is not just a classroom concept — it underpins a vast range of modern technology. Loudspeakers work by sending a varying electrical current through a coil (attached to a paper cone) that sits inside a permanent magnet. As the current changes direction and magnitude, the motor-effect force on the coil changes, pushing the cone in and out and creating sound waves.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scanners used in hospitals contain powerful electromagnets that produce extremely strong, uniform magnetic fields. These align the magnetic properties of hydrogen atoms in the body, and by measuring how those atoms re-emit energy, detailed images of soft tissue can be produced without using ionising radiation. The strength of an MRI magnet is measured in tesla — clinical scanners typically use fields of 1.5 T to 3 T, far stronger than anything achievable with permanent magnets of practical size. This illustrates how electromagnetic principles developed in physics laboratories have direct, life-saving medical applications.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions on Fleming’s left-hand rule, always identify all three quantities (force, field, current) before answering. A common mistake is using the right hand instead of the left — Fleming’s left-hand rule is for the motor effect. For ‘Suggest’ questions about increasing the force on a conductor, link each suggestion directly to the equation \(F = BIl\) — examiners reward causal language, not just lists.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Like poles repel; unlike poles attract. Induced magnets are temporary and always attract the magnet that induces them. Electromagnets can be switched on and off and have adjustable strength.
  • The motor effect: a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force (F = BIl). Force is greatest at right angles to the field.
  • Fleming’s left-hand rule gives the force direction: Thumb = Motion, First finger = Field (N to S), Second finger = Current (+ to -). Electric motors use this effect to produce continuous rotation via a split-ring commutator.

practice_questions.text: A wire carrying a current of 3 A is placed at right angles to a magnetic field with flux density 0.5 T. The length of wire in the field is 0.2 m. Calculate the force on the wire. Suggest what would happen to the force if the current were doubled.

Mastering: Suggests the force would double to 0.6 N because F is directly proportional to I in F = BIl (1 mark). Identifies this is because current squared does not appear — only linear dependence on I (1 mark). [4 marks]

Mastering: Suggests a specific application such as a scrapyard crane (picking up and releasing metal objects) or an MRI scanner (field must be very strong and controllable) and explains why on/off capability is essential — releasing the object requires the field to be removed instantly (1 mark). [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Electric motors are used in many everyday devices, from washing machines to electric vehicles. Evaluate the scientific principles that make the electric motor work and consider how changes in design could improve its performance.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Identifies that the motor uses a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field.
Developing: Explains the motor effect using F = BIl — a force acts on the current-carrying sides of the coil (1 mark). Describes the role of the split-ring commutator in maintaining continuous rotation by reversing current every half turn (1 mark).
Secure: Uses Fleming’s left-hand rule to explain why opposite sides of the coil experience forces in opposite directions, creating a turning effect (torque) (1 mark). glossary_terms.definition: A magnet that produces its own magnetic field at all times, without needing an external current or field.
A magnetic material that only becomes a magnet when placed inside an external magnetic field, losing its magnetism when removed.
Materials that are attracted to magnets and can be magnetised, such as iron, steel, nickel and cobalt.
The region around a magnet where a magnetic material or moving charge experiences a force.
A coil of wire that produces a strong, uniform magnetic field inside it when current flows through it. Its field pattern resembles that of a bar magnet.
A solenoid with a soft iron core, producing a strong magnet that can be switched on and off with the current.
The force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field, caused by the interaction between the conductor's own field and the external field.
A measure of the strength of a magnetic field, measured in tesla (T).
A rule for finding the direction of force on a current-carrying conductor: thumb = thrust (force direction), first finger = field direction (N to S), second finger = conventional current direction.
